:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Today's Lecture
:::
In today's lecture we will cover:

-   A new kind of problem: learning without a target
-   Person-centered and variable-centered questions
-   A brief history of K-means
-   Distance, centroids, and within-cluster variation
-   The K-means algorithm, step by step and in R
-   Random starts and local optima
-   Choosing K: the elbow and the silhouette
-   K-means on the personality data
-   Describing, validating, and reporting clusters
-   When K-means fails
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Where We Have Been
:::

Every method so far had a target. Linear and logistic regression, the lasso,
decision trees, random forests, and boosting all learned to predict $y$ from
$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_p$.

That is **supervised learning**. We had an answer key, so we could hold out
a test set and score each model on data it had not seen.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Today there is no $y$.
:::

We have the same kind of data, $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_p$ measured on $n$ people,
but no outcome to predict. The question changes from "how well can we predict
$y$" to "what structure is in these variables."
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Unsupervised Learning
:::

Two families of unsupervised methods, and this module covers both.

-   **Clustering** looks for groups of similar observations. The output is a
    new categorical variable: which group each person belongs to.
-   **Dimension reduction** looks for a small number of new variables that
    carry most of the information in the original ones. Principal components
    analysis is the classic example, and it comes in two weeks.

There is no test set error to compute, because there is no answer to compare
to. Evaluation rests on internal consistency, stability across samples, and
whether the result is useful.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Unsupervised learning is closer to exploratory data analysis than to
prediction. A cluster solution is the start of a hypothesis, not a verdict.
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Two Kinds of Questions
:::

| | Variable-centered | Person-centered |
|----|----|----|
| **Asks** | How do the variables relate across the whole sample? | Are there subgroups of people with distinct patterns? |
| **Assumes** | One model applies to everyone | The population is a mix of types |
| **Good for** | Describing dimensions, estimating effects, testing mechanisms | Typologies, tailoring interventions, finding hidden subpopulations |
| **Risk** | Averages over subgroups that differ | Solutions can be unstable and depend on the method |
| **Output** | New variables built from the old ones, with a loading for each variable | A group label for each person |
| **Methods** | Regression, PCA, factor analysis | Cluster analysis, mixture models |

Clustering is person-centered: each person gets a label. Dimension reduction,
which starts in two weeks with PCA, is variable-centered: it works on the
columns, not the rows, and each variable gets a loading. The two approaches
are complementary, and the same dataset often deserves both.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Why Psychologists Cluster
:::

-   **Personality profiles.** Are there types of people, not just dimensions?
    The resilient, overcontrolled, and undercontrolled profiles reported by
    Robins and colleagues (1996) and Asendorpf and colleagues (2001) came from
    clustering Big Five scores.
-   **Symptom subtypes.** Do people with the same diagnosis fall into groups
    with different symptom patterns, and do the groups respond to treatment
    differently?
-   **Patterns of daily life.** In experience sampling data, are there typical
    days, or typical people, defined by how mood, sleep, and activity go
    together?
-   **Segments.** Students by how they engage with a course, patients by how
    they use services, customers by what they buy.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
A clustering algorithm always returns clusters, whether or not real groups
exist. Deciding whether the groups are real is the hard part of the analysis.
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}

:::

Pick a construct from your own area: a disorder, a personality trait, a

-   Do you think it comes in **types**, or does it vary along a
    **continuum**?
-   What would you need to see in data to be convinced the types are real,
    and not just cuts along a continuum?
-   If the types were real, who would use them, and what would they do
    differently?

Hold onto your answers. The second question comes back in the group
activity near the end of the lecture.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## A Brief History of K-Means
:::

::: {style="color: lightblue"}
**Independent discoveries, 1956 to 1967**
:::

-   Hugo Steinhaus (1956) described partitioning points into $k$ groups to
    minimize within-group variance.
-   Stuart Lloyd (1957) wrote the assign-and-update algorithm in a Bell Labs
    report on signal quantization. It was not published until 1982.
-   James MacQueen (1967) independently proposed a similar procedure and gave
    it the name **k-means**.

::: {style="color: lightblue"}
**The algorithm R uses**
:::

-   John Hartigan and Manchek Wong (1979) published a faster version that
    moves single points between clusters. It is the default in R's
    `kmeans()`.
-   K-means is now in every statistics package and is the baseline that other
    clustering methods are compared against.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Measuring Similarity
:::

Clustering needs a definition of "close." K-means uses **Euclidean
distance**, the straight-line distance between two rows of the data:

$$
d(x_i, x_{i'}) = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p} (x_{ij} - x_{i'j})^2}
$$

-   A variable measured in big units dominates the distance. Age in years will
    swamp a 1 to 5 rating scale. **Standardize the variables first** unless
    they are already on the same scale.
-   Other distances exist: Manhattan, Gower for mixed numeric and categorical
    data, and correlation-based distances. K-means is tied to Euclidean
    distance. Hierarchical clustering, next lecture, can use any of them.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Defining a Cluster
:::

A cluster $C_k$ is a set of observations, summarized by its **centroid**
$\mu_k$, the mean of its members on every variable.

The **within-cluster variation** of $C_k$ is the sum of squared distances
from its members to its centroid:

$$
W(C_k) = \sum_{i \in C_k} \| x_i - \mu_k \|^2
$$

The **total within-cluster sum of squares** adds this over all $K$ clusters:

$$
SS_{\text{within}} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} W(C_k)
$$

K-means looks for the assignment of observations to clusters that makes
$SS_{\text{within}}$ as small as possible. Smaller means tighter clusters.
Since $SS_{\text{total}} = SS_{\text{within}} + SS_{\text{between}}$, the
ratio $SS_{\text{between}} / SS_{\text{total}}$ works like an $R^2$ for the
clustering.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## The K-Means Algorithm
:::

1.  Choose $K$, the number of clusters.
2.  Pick $K$ starting centroids, usually $K$ randomly chosen observations.
3.  **Assignment step.** Assign each observation to its nearest centroid.
4.  **Update step.** Move each centroid to the mean of the observations now
    assigned to it.
5.  Repeat steps 3 and 4 until no assignment changes.

Neither step can increase $SS_{\text{within}}$, so the algorithm always
settles. It settles at a **local** minimum, which depends on where it
started. We will see what that means in a moment.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Watch It Run
:::

Naftali Harris built an interactive page that runs the algorithm one step at
a time:

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
<https://www.naftaliharris.com/blog/visualizing-k-means-clustering/>
:::

How to use it in class:

1.  Pick **I'll Choose** for the centroids and **Gaussian Mixture** for the
    data, then click to place three centroids badly, all in one corner.
2.  Alternate **Reassign Points** and **Update Centroids**. Each pair of
    clicks is one iteration. Watch the centroids drift toward the groups and
    the assignments settle.
3.  Reset with **Randomly** chosen centroids and run it a few times. Different
    starts land in different places, which is the local optimum problem we
    look at next.
4.  Try the **Smiley Face** and **Packed Circles** data. K-means cannot find
    those shapes, and we come back to why at the end.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Load the Required Packages
:::

```{r}
library(dplyr)       # data manipulation and the pipe
library(tidyr)       # pivot_longer() for the profile plot
library(ggplot2)     # plots
library(cluster)     # silhouette()
library(factoextra)  # fviz_nbclust() and fviz_cluster()
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### K-Means in a Few Lines of R
:::

Here is the whole algorithm on three made-up groups of points. The starting
centroids are deliberately bad: all three come from the same group.

```{r}
set.seed(559)
true_centers <- data.frame(x = c(-3, 3, 0), y = c(0, 0, 4))
blobs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(k)
  data.frame(x = rnorm(60, true_centers$x[k]), y = rnorm(60, true_centers$y[k]))))

X <- as.matrix(blobs)
K <- 3
centroids <- X[order(X[, "x"])[1:K], ]   # the three leftmost points
snapshots <- list()

for (it in 1:30) {
  # assignment step: squared distance from every point to every centroid
  d <- sapply(1:K, function(k) rowSums((X - matrix(centroids[k, ], nrow(X), 2, byrow = TRUE))^2))
  cluster <- max.col(-d)                 # the nearest centroid
  snapshots[[it]] <- data.frame(blobs, cluster = factor(cluster), iteration = it,
                                cx = centroids[cluster, 1], cy = centroids[cluster, 2])
  # update step: move each centroid to the mean of its members
  new_centroids <- t(sapply(1:K, function(k) colMeans(X[cluster == k, , drop = FALSE])))
  if (all(abs(new_centroids - centroids) < 1e-8)) break
  centroids <- new_centroids
}
length(snapshots)
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Watching K-Means Converge
:::

Crosses are the centroids at the start of each iteration. Even from a bad
start, the centroids spread out and find the three groups in
`r length(snapshots)` iterations.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.6
shown <- do.call(rbind, snapshots[c(1, 2, 3, length(snapshots))])
shown$iteration <- factor(paste("Iteration", shown$iteration),
                          levels = unique(paste("Iteration", shown$iteration)))
centers_shown <- unique(shown[, c("iteration", "cluster", "cx", "cy")])

ggplot(shown, aes(x, y, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = centers_shown, aes(cx, cy, color = cluster),
             shape = 4, size = 6, stroke = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ iteration, nrow = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## K-Means Finds a Local Optimum
:::

With more clusters, a single random start can settle somewhere poor. Here are
nine groups on a grid, clustered with $K = 9$ from twelve different random
starts. The number reported is $SS_{\text{within}}$, so lower is better.

```{r}
set.seed(559)
grid9 <- expand.grid(x = c(-5, 0, 5), y = c(-5, 0, 5))
nine  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:9, function(k)
  data.frame(x = rnorm(40, grid9$x[k], 0.8), y = rnorm(40, grid9$y[k], 0.8))))

one_start <- sapply(1:12, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  kmeans(nine, centers = 9, nstart = 1, iter.max = 50)$tot.withinss
})
round(one_start)
```

The same data and the same $K$ give answers that differ by a factor of three,
depending only on the random start.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### A Bad Solution Looks Fine Until You See It
:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
worst <- which.max(one_start)
set.seed(worst); km_bad  <- kmeans(nine, centers = 9, nstart = 1,  iter.max = 50)
set.seed(559);   km_good <- kmeans(nine, centers = 9, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)

both <- rbind(
  data.frame(nine, cluster = factor(km_bad$cluster),
             run = paste0("One random start, SS within = ", round(km_bad$tot.withinss))),
  data.frame(nine, cluster = factor(km_good$cluster),
             run = paste0("Best of 25 starts, SS within = ", round(km_good$tot.withinss))))

ggplot(both, aes(x, y, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ run) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

In the poor solution, some groups have been split in two while neighboring
groups share a centroid. Nothing in the printed output warns you.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Random Starts
:::

The fix is simple: run the algorithm many times from different random starts
and keep the solution with the smallest $SS_{\text{within}}$. The `nstart`
argument does this for you.

```{r}
set.seed(559)
kmeans(nine, centers = 9, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)$tot.withinss
```

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Use `nstart = 25` or more, and set a seed before `kmeans()` so the solution
can be reproduced. The default, `nstart = 1`, is almost never what you want.
:::

`iter.max` caps the number of assign-and-update rounds. The default of 10 is
sometimes too few and R will warn you. Raising it to 50 costs nothing.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## `kmeans()` in R
:::

```r
kmeans(x, centers, nstart = 1, iter.max = 10)
```

| Argument | What it does |
|----|----|
| `x` | A numeric matrix or data frame. Standardize it first. |
| `centers` | The number of clusters $K$, or a matrix of starting centroids. |
| `nstart` | How many random starts to try. Keep the best. |
| `iter.max` | Maximum assign-and-update rounds per start. |

The result is a list. The pieces you will use:

| Element | Contents |
|----|----|
| `cluster` | The cluster each observation was assigned to. |
| `centers` | A $K \times p$ matrix of centroids. |
| `size` | How many observations are in each cluster. |
| `withinss`, `tot.withinss` | $W(C_k)$ for each cluster, and their sum. |
| `betweenss`, `totss` | $SS_{\text{between}}$ and $SS_{\text{total}}$. |
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## The Personality Data Again
:::

The same Big Five data as the tree lectures: 1,000 people who answered 50
IPIP items on a 1 to 5 scale. In the supervised lectures we predicted one item
from the other 49. Today we ask a person-centered question instead.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Are there types of people in these data, defined by their pattern across the
five traits?
:::

Three preparation steps come first, and each one is a decision you would
report in a paper.

1.  Handle missing data. A 0 means the item was skipped.
2.  Reverse the negatively keyed items and average each trait's ten items into
    a trait score.
3.  Standardize the five trait scores.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Step 1: Prepare the Data
:::

```{r}
data <- readRDS("data/data-final.RDS")
dim(data)

# a 0 means the item was skipped, so keep only complete rows
complete <- apply(data, 1, function(r) all(r %in% 1:5))
data <- data[complete, ]
dim(data)

negatively_keyed <- c("EXT2", "EXT4", "EXT6", "EXT8", "EXT10", "EST2", "EST4",
                      "AGR1", "AGR3", "AGR5", "AGR7", "CSN2", "CSN4", "CSN6", "CSN8",
                      "OPN2", "OPN4", "OPN6")
data[negatively_keyed] <- 6 - data[negatively_keyed]

traits <- data.frame(
  Extraversion      = rowMeans(data[grep("^EXT", names(data))]),
  Neuroticism       = rowMeans(data[grep("^EST", names(data))]),
  Agreeableness     = rowMeans(data[grep("^AGR", names(data))]),
  Conscientiousness = rowMeans(data[grep("^CSN", names(data))]),
  Openness          = rowMeans(data[grep("^OPN", names(data))]))
round(head(traits, 4), 2)
```

The EST items are keyed so that a high score means more emotional
instability, which is why the trait is labeled Neuroticism.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Standardize Before Clustering
:::

The five traits are all on a 1 to 5 scale, but their spreads differ. Openness
and Agreeableness vary less across people than Extraversion does, so without
standardizing, Extraversion would get more say in the distances.

```{r}
round(sapply(traits, sd), 2)

traits_z <- scale(traits)
round(apply(traits_z, 2, sd), 2)
```

Every variable now has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, so each
trait contributes equally to the Euclidean distance between two people.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Step 2: How Many Clusters?
:::

K-means needs $K$ before it starts. Two common tools, neither of which is
decisive.

::: {style="color: lightblue"}
**The elbow method**
:::

Fit K-means for $K = 1, 2, \dots, 10$ and plot $SS_{\text{within}}$ against
$K$. It always goes down as $K$ grows. Look for the point where the drops
stop being worth it.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
set.seed(559)
fviz_nbclust(traits_z, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 10, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)
```

There is no clear elbow here. That is the usual outcome with real data.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### The Silhouette
:::

The silhouette asks, for each person $i$, whether they sit closer to their
own cluster than to the next one.

-   $a(i)$: the mean distance from $i$ to the other members of its own
    cluster. This measures **cohesion**.
-   $b(i)$: the mean distance from $i$ to the members of the nearest other
    cluster. This measures **separation**.

$$
s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\{a(i), b(i)\}}
$$

$s(i)$ runs from $-1$ to $1$. Near 1 means well placed, near 0 means on the
border between two clusters, and negative means probably in the wrong one.
The **average silhouette** over everyone summarizes the solution. A rough
guide from Kaufman and Rousseeuw: above 0.5 is reasonable structure, 0.25 to
0.5 is weak, and below 0.25 is little evidence of distinct groups.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Silhouette for the Personality Data
:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8
set.seed(559)
fviz_nbclust(traits_z, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 10, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
set.seed(559)
sil_k <- sapply(2:10, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(traits_z, centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 50)
  mean(silhouette(km$cluster, dist(traits_z))[, 3])
})
```

The average silhouette peaks at $K = `r which.max(sil_k) + 1`$ at
`r round(max(sil_k), 2)`, and never rises above 0.2. By the rule of thumb,
that is weak evidence of distinct types. This is normal for personality
traits, which behave more like continuous dimensions than categories.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Choosing K Is a Judgment Call
:::

The elbow plot gives no answer, and the silhouette weakly prefers two
clusters. Two clusters here would split people into "high on everything
desirable" and "low," which is not very interesting.

We will fit $K = 3$, for two reasons:

-   Three-cluster solutions are interpretable and match the profiles reported
    in the personality literature.
-   The silhouette for $K = 3$ is barely different from $K = 2$, so the
    statistics do not object.

Then we will check whether the three-cluster solution **replicates** in
random halves of the data. That check is worth more than either index.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Report what the indices said and why you chose what you chose. Readers can
disagree with a judgment they can see. They cannot evaluate one that is hidden.
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Step 3: Fit the Final Model
:::

```{r}
set.seed(559)
km <- kmeans(traits_z, centers = 3, nstart = 50, iter.max = 50)

km$size
round(km$betweenss / km$totss, 2)
```

The three clusters explain about `r round(100 * km$betweenss / km$totss)`
percent of the total variation in the five trait scores. The rest is variation
within clusters: people in the same cluster are still quite different from
each other.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Step 4: Describe the Clusters
:::

The centroids are the cluster means on each standardized trait. A value of
0.5 means that cluster averages half a standard deviation above the sample on
that trait.

```{r}
knitr::kable(round(km$centers, 2))
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### The Profiles
:::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
profiles <- as.data.frame(km$centers) %>%
  mutate(cluster = paste0("Cluster ", 1:n(), " (n = ", km$size, ")")) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "trait", values_to = "z")

ggplot(profiles, aes(trait, z, fill = trait)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ cluster) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Cluster mean (z score)")
```

Which cluster gets which number is arbitrary. Run it with a different seed
and the labels can switch while the profiles stay the same. You will put
names on these three patterns yourselves in the group activity later on.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Seeing the Clusters in Two Dimensions
:::

Five traits cannot be plotted directly. `fviz_cluster()` projects the data
onto its first two principal components, which is a preview of the dimension
reduction lectures. The clusters touch, which is what a silhouette below 0.2
looks like.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
fviz_cluster(km, data = traits_z, geom = "point", ellipse.type = "convex",
             ggtheme = theme_minimal())
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Step 5: Does the Solution Replicate?
:::

If the three profiles are real, they should show up in any random half of
the sample, not just in this particular set of people. A simple check:

1.  Split the sample into two random halves, A and B.
2.  Run K-means separately in each half, with the same $K$ and settings.
3.  Compare the two solutions. If the same three profiles appear in both
    halves, the solution replicates.

Cluster numbers are arbitrary, so the first job is to work out which cluster
in half B corresponds to which cluster in half A. We pair each half A
centroid with the half B centroid that is closest to it.

```{r}
set.seed(559)
half <- sample(nrow(traits_z), nrow(traits_z) %/% 2)
A <- traits_z[half, ]
B <- traits_z[-half, ]

set.seed(1); km_A <- kmeans(A, centers = 3, nstart = 50, iter.max = 50)
set.seed(2); km_B <- kmeans(B, centers = 3, nstart = 50, iter.max = 50)

# for each half A centroid, the number of the closest half B centroid
match_B <- apply(km_A$centers, 1, function(center_A)
  which.min(colSums((t(km_B$centers) - center_A)^2)))
match_B
```

Half A's cluster `r names(match_B)[1]` matches half B's cluster
`r match_B[1]`, and so on. The numbers differ but the pairing is one to one.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### The Same Profiles in Both Halves
:::

Here are the centroids from each half, with half B's rows reordered so that
matched clusters sit on the same line.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {}
**Half A**
```{r}
knitr::kable(round(km_A$centers, 2))
```
:::
::: {}
**Half B, reordered to match**
```{r}
knitr::kable(round(km_B$centers[match_B, ], 2))
```
:::
::::

Read across each row: the same traits are high and low in both halves. All
three patterns appear in both halves of the data, found independently.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Do People Land in the Same Cluster?
:::

A stricter check works at the level of people. For each person in half B,
ask two questions: which half A centroid are they closest to, and which half
B cluster did K-means put them in? If the two solutions agree, those two
labels should match for most people.

```{r}
# for each row of x, the number of the closest centroid
nearest_centroid <- function(x, centers) {
  d <- sapply(1:nrow(centers), function(k)
    rowSums((x - matrix(centers[k, ], nrow(x), ncol(x), byrow = TRUE))^2))
  max.col(-d)
}

label_from_A <- nearest_centroid(B, km_A$centers)   # labels in half A's numbering
label_from_A <- match_B[label_from_A]               # translated to half B's numbering
label_from_B <- km_B$cluster

table(label_from_A, label_from_B)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
agree_rate <- mean(label_from_A == label_from_B)
```

Each row should pile up on the diagonal, and it does. Overall,
`r round(100 * agree_rate)` percent of people in half B get the same label
whichever half's centroids are used. The profiles are stable, even though
they are not sharply separated.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Using the Cluster Variable
:::

After clustering, each person has a new categorical variable: their cluster.
That variable can go into any analysis you already know.

-   **Describe** the clusters on variables that were not used to form them:
    age, sex, education, diagnoses, outcomes.
-   **Test** whether the clusters differ on those variables with ANOVA,
    chi-square tests, or regression with cluster as a predictor.
-   **Predict** cluster membership from other variables, or use membership to
    predict an outcome.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Differences on variables that were not used in the clustering are the
strongest evidence that a typology means something. Differences on the
clustering variables themselves are guaranteed and prove nothing.
:::

These data have no external variables, which is why the replication check
had to carry the weight.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Four Ways to Justify a Cluster Solution
:::

1.  **Conceptual.** The profiles make sense and connect to theory or prior
    work.
2.  **Internal criteria.** The elbow, the silhouette, and
    $SS_{\text{between}} / SS_{\text{total}}$ for the chosen $K$ against its
    neighbors.
3.  **Replication.** The same profiles appear in random halves, or in a new
    sample.
4.  **External differentiation.** The clusters differ on variables not used
    to build them.

No single one of these is enough. A paper that reports all four, including
the ones that came out weak, is more convincing than one that reports a
single index that happened to agree.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Small Group Activity: Interpreting the Clusters
:::

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
In groups of three or four, take ten minutes on the questions below. Pick one
person to report back. Use the centroid table, the profile plot, the
silhouette, and the split-half tables as your evidence.
:::

1.  **Name the profiles.** Give each of the three clusters a name of two or
    three words. For each name, point to the centroid values that support it,
    and say which value, if any, makes you hesitate.
2.  **Defend the number.** The silhouette preferred two clusters and we fit
    three. What would you need to see in the data, or in the literature, to
    argue for two instead? For four?
3.  **Fix the sentence.** A colleague writes, "The three clusters explain
    `r round(100 * km$betweenss / km$totss)` percent of personality." What is
    wrong with that sentence, and how would you rewrite it?
4.  **Make it testable.** Suppose you could add one variable that was not
    used in the clustering, such as life satisfaction, GPA, or a clinical
    diagnosis. How would you use it to test whether the typology matters,
    and what result would convince you that it does not?
5.  **Change the inputs.** What would you expect to change if we clustered on
    the 50 items instead of the 5 trait scores? If we skipped standardizing?
    Which of those choices is a judgment call and which is a mistake?

::: {style="color: lightblue"}
When we come back together, each group reports its three names from question
1 and its answer to question 4.
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## When K-Means Fails
:::

K-means works well when the clusters are roughly round, roughly the same
size, and separated in Euclidean distance. Its assumptions are easy to break.

-   **Shape.** Every cluster is a ball around its centroid. Elongated, curved,
    or nested groups get cut into pieces.
-   **Size.** Large spread-out groups lose their edges to small tight ones.
-   **Outliers.** A few extreme points drag a centroid toward them, or claim a
    cluster of their own.
-   **Scale.** Unstandardized variables with large units dominate.
-   **Everyone belongs.** Each observation is forced into a cluster, even if it
    is nothing like the others.
-   **K is fixed in advance.** The algorithm cannot tell you it should have
    been a different number.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Two Rings
:::

Two rings, one inside the other, are two obvious groups. K-means cannot see
them because no centroid can sit at the middle of a ring.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
set.seed(559)
n  <- 150
t1 <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
t2 <- runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
rings <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = cos(t1) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.10),     y = sin(t1) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.10),     ring = "inner"),
  data.frame(x = 3 * cos(t2) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.15), y = 3 * sin(t2) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.15), ring = "outer"))

set.seed(559)
rings$cluster <- factor(kmeans(rings[, c("x", "y")], centers = 2, nstart = 25)$cluster)

ggplot(rings, aes(x, y, color = cluster, shape = ring)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()
```

K-means slices the picture in half. Hierarchical clustering with single
linkage, density-based methods such as DBSCAN, and model-based clustering can
all handle shapes like this. They are the next two lectures.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Reporting a Cluster Analysis
:::

There is no standard format for reporting cluster analyses in psychology, so
be explicit. A reader should be able to reproduce the solution and judge it.

-   The variables clustered on, and how they were scaled.
-   The distance measure and the algorithm, with the seed and `nstart`.
-   How $K$ was chosen, including the indices that disagreed.
-   Cluster sizes and centroids, with a profile plot. Any names you give
    the clusters are interpretations, so report the centroids and let the
    names follow from them.
-   Evidence for the solution: replication, and differences on external
    variables.
-   The honest caveat: the algorithm would have produced clusters either way,
    and the solution is a description of this sample, not a discovery of
    natural kinds.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Cluster solutions are hypotheses. The test of a typology is whether it
replicates in new data and predicts something that matters.
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Summary
:::

-   Unsupervised learning has no target, so there is no test set score. We
    judge solutions by stability, interpretability, and usefulness.
-   K-means assigns each observation to the nearest of $K$ centroids and moves
    the centroids to the means of their members, repeating until nothing
    changes. It minimizes within-cluster sum of squares.
-   It finds a local optimum. Use many random starts and a seed.
-   Standardize first. Choose $K$ with the elbow, the silhouette, and
    judgment, then check that the solution replicates.
-   K-means assumes round clusters of similar size and forces every point into
    one. When that fails, other methods are needed.

::: {style="color: lightblue"}
**Next time:** hierarchical clustering. No $K$ in advance, any distance
measure, and a dendrogram that shows the whole family of solutions at once.
:::
::::
